From the boardroom to the backlog, the pressure is relentless. But here’s the uncomfortable truth most PMs won’t say out loud — the majority of AI features shipped today don’t solve real user problems. They solve internal optics problems. They exist because someone important asked, “Where’s our AI strategy?” This article gives you a practical, reusable framework — the IMPACT model — for deciding where to embed AI in your existing product, how deep to integrate it, and when to say no . The AI Integration Dilemma McKinsey’s 2024 Global AI Survey found that 72% of organizations now use AI in at least one business function — up from 55% a year earlier. Yet Gartner simultaneously reports that over 85% of AI projects fail to deliver business value. The gap between adoption and impact is the PM’s real problem. Press enter or click to view image in full size The root cause is almost always the same: teams start with the technology (“We should use LLMs”) instead of the user problem (“Customers abandon our onboarding flow at step 3”). This is solution-first thinking, and it’s the single biggest predictor of AI features that ship and die. A 2025 Harvard Business Review study found that products where AI was embedded to solve a measured user pain point saw 3.2x higher feature adoption than products where AI was added as a capability upgrade. The difference wasn’t the AI — it was the problem definition. The IMPACT Framework IMPACT is a six-step decision model that forces you to validate the problem before you commit to the solution . Each letter represents a gate — pass all six, and you have a high-confidence AI integration candidate. Fail any one, and you’ve saved your team months of wasted effort. I — Identify the Pain M — Measure the Manual P — Prove the Accuracy A — Assess the Cost-to-Value C — Choose the Integration Depth T — Test with Real Users Press enter or click to view image in full size Let’s walk through each step with real-world examples. Step 1: Identify the Pain Before you write a single user story involving AI, answer one question: What specific user problem will this solve, and how do users solve it today? Spotify didn’t build Discover Weekly because “AI recommendation engines” were trending. They built it because users spent an average of 30 minutes browsing before finding something to play — and 25% gave up entirely. The pain was measurable, specific, and worth solving. The litmus test: Can you complete this sentence? “Users currently spend [X time/effort] doing [specific task], and [Y%] of them [fail/abandon/complain] because [specific reason].” If you can’t fill in those blanks with data, you don’t have a problem statement — you have a hypothesis. Go validate it first. Step 2: Measure the Manual Once you’ve identified a real pain point, quantify the human effort currently burned on it. This is where most PM business cases for AI live or die. Amazon’s Q Developer is a masterclass in this step. Before building their AI coding assistant, Amazon measured that upgrading 30,000 Java applications from JDK 8/11 to JDK 17 would require an estimated 4,500 developer-years of manual effort. The AI alternative completed the same work with 79% of changes approved without human modification. That’s a business case no executive can argue with. Key metrics to capture: Hours per task (manual baseline) Error rate in manual execution Volume of repetitive decisions per day/week Cost of delay when humans are the bottleneck If the manual effort is low or the task is infrequent, AI integration probably isn’t worth the complexity it introduces. Step 3: Prove the Accuracy This is the gate where most AI features should die — and don’t, because teams skip it. The question isn’t “Can AI do this task?” It’s “Can AI do this task at or above the accuracy threshold our users will tolerate?” Google Health’s AI mammography system passed this gate brilliantly. Before shipping, they proved that AI-assisted screening detected 20% more cancers than traditional double-reading by radiologists while cutting workload by 44%. The accuracy bar wasn’t “AI can read mammograms” — it was “AI catches cancers that two trained radiologists missed.” Contrast this with early chatbot deployments where companies shipped AI with 60–70% accuracy into customer support — and watched satisfaction scores crater. Stanford’s research found that developers using AI coding assistants produced significantly less secure code yet felt more confident. Accuracy theater is worse than no AI at all. The accuracy test: Run your AI solution against a golden dataset of 500+ real examples. If it doesn’t beat human performance on the metric that matters to users, it’s not ready.
